text:
[15] Essential Social Media Stories for Professionals
https://t.co/g2mjT3MUUt

According to Press Monitor's media intelligence tracking of Indian publications, this press review covers 15 essential stories — news on social media regulation, platform accountability, and digital discourse. From regulatory actions to corporate disputes, these stories define the evolving relationship between social platforms and Indian society.

1. Mann Wife Defamation Restraint
A front-page report in Times of India says a district court in Chandigarh Wednesday restrained SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia, Congress MLA Sukhpal Singh Khaira and retired Punjab and Haryana High Court judge Justice Ranjit Singh from posting unverified or allegedly defamatory material against Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann's wife Dr Gurpreet Kaur on social media or any other medium until further orders. The court passed the interim order while hearing a defamation petition filed by Kaur against the three respondents on September 8, relating to allegations that she had demanded Rs 5 crore to help suppress a rape case. The next hearing is scheduled for September 30.
Why it matters: The Chandigarh court's interim order sets a significant precedent for online speech boundaries involving public figures in Indian politics. Key detail: Three respondents — SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia, Congress MLA Sukhpal Singh Khaira, and retired judge Justice Ranjit Singh — are barred until further orders, with the next hearing on September 30. Source: Times of India and Tribune. Next step: Political offices across India will likely issue social media compliance guidelines. Closing: Will this ruling reshape how politicians and their supporters engage on digital platforms?

2. Meta Executives Appear Before NCPCR
A front-page report in Financial Express says senior executives of Meta appeared before the National Child Rights Protection Council on Wednesday in connection with the inquiry into alleged advertisements featuring child sexual exploitation and abuse material on the platform.
Why it matters: This appearance signals tightening regulatory scrutiny of global social media platforms operating in India, reinforcing the need for robust media monitoring. Key detail: Senior Meta executives discussed alleged child sexual exploitation advertisements on the platform with the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights. Source: Financial Express and The Pioneer. Next step: Expect Meta to announce enhanced content moderation policies for the Indian market. Closing: How will global platforms balance free expression with child protection obligations?

3. Meta Faces New Mexico Privacy Lawsuit
A front-page report in The Pioneer says New Mexico will begin opening statements on Wednesday in Santa Fe state court against Meta over privacy violations tied to user data harvested during the twenty sixteen election for targeted advertising. State Attorney General Raul Torrez highlighted that the social media giant's actions exposed a consistent pattern of misrepresenting how user information was collected. While forty eight other United States states recently reached a landmark settlement with the company, New Mexico pursued independent legal action alongside Florida, which also declined to join the broader agreement.
Why it matters: New Mexico's independent legal action against Meta over 2016 election data harvesting shows that state-level privacy enforcement is gaining momentum globally. Key detail: While 48 US states reached a landmark settlement, New Mexico and Florida pursued separate legal action, highlighting persistent concerns about user data misuse. Source: The Pioneer. Next step: Monitor for similar state-level actions that could influence Indian data protection debates. Closing: Can state-level litigation force meaningful change in how social platforms handle user data?

4. Subhash Chandra Sues Social Media Platforms
A front-page report in Business Line says Subhash Chandra, founder of Zee Entertainment Enterprises, has sent letters threatening to sue Meta, YouTube, X, and LinkedIn India for defamation over content about his personal insolvency case. He gave the platforms a week to correct information about a repayment plan approved by the National Company Law Tribunal. Chandra claims his borrowing was nil and he was only a personal guarantor.
Why it matters: Zee Entertainment founder Subhash Chandra's defamation threat against Meta, YouTube, X, and LinkedIn India underscores the growing use of legal action against social platforms in India. Key detail: Chandra claims his borrowing was nil and he was only a personal guarantor, disputing reports about his insolvency case. Source: Business Line. Next step: Watch for platform responses and potential legal counterarguments. Closing: Will defamation claims become a new tool for shaping online discourse?

5. Delhi Airport Fake Waterlogging Video FIR
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says police registered an FIR against 63 social media handles for circulating a misleading video claiming waterlogging at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport was actually old footage from Dubai. The case, filed on September 6, invoked sections of the BNS and IT Act accusing the operators of spreading misinformation to defame a critical public utility. Authorities clarified that while heavy rainfall caused temporary water accumulation at Terminal 3's arrival forecourt, operations were never affected and the situation was resolved within 20 minutes.
Why it matters: Police action against 63 social media handles demonstrates authorities' increasing willingness to pursue misinformation targeting critical public infrastructure. Key detail: An old Dubai airport waterlogging video was falsely claimed as Delhi airport footage; operations were never affected and resolved within 20 minutes. Source: Hindustan Times and The Pioneer. Next step: Expect more FIRs under the IT Act as viral misinformation continues to spread. Closing: How can social media users verify content before sharing it with their networks?

6. Singapore Questions Five Over Racist Posts
A front-page report in The Pioneer says that Singapore police have questioned five individuals aged between twenty nine and sixty six regarding racist and xenophobic online comments about the Nepal floods and Singapore Airlines investment in Air India. Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam condemned the remarks, noting they incite hostility despite thousands affected by the disaster. Authorities are actively investigating the cases and have urged social media platforms to remove content violating community guidelines.
Why it matters: Singapore's enforcement against racist online comments about Nepal floods and Air India investment shows growing global accountability for social media speech. Key detail: Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam condemned remarks inciting hostility, and authorities urged platforms to remove violating content. Source: The Pioneer. Next step: Watch for cross-border cooperation on social media regulation. Closing: Should racist online speech face international consequences?

7. Ajit Mohan Steps Down as Snapchat CBO
A front-page report in Business Standard says Snapchat’s chief business officer Ajit Mohan has decided to step down after four years, citing personal reasons to return to India. Ronan Harris will replace him as CBO at Snap, and Mohan will remain at the company until the end of the calendar year.
Why it matters: Leadership changes at major social platforms directly impact advertising strategies and monetization in key markets like India. Key detail: Ajit Mohan steps down after four years citing personal reasons to return to India; Ronan Harris will replace him as CBO. Source: Business Standard. Next step: Monitor Snap's India advertising strategy under new leadership. Closing: What does this mean for Snapchat's growth in the Indian market?

8. Saadia Azim's Book on Disinformation
A front-page report in Business Standard says Saadia Azim's book Forwarded as Received examines the spread of misinformation and disinformation in contemporary India. The book highlights how fake news has led to real-world violence, including the lynching of Mohammad Akhlaq in Uttar Pradesh in 2015. Azim argues that rebuilding trust and digital literacy, rather than censorship, is the way forward.
Why it matters: Saadia Azim's Forwarded as Received offers a compelling framework for combating disinformation through digital literacy rather than censorship — a critical conversation for media intelligence. Key detail: The book highlights how fake news led to real-world violence, including the lynching of Mohammad Akhlaq in 2015, and proposes prebunking mechanisms. Source: Business Standard. Next step: Expect broader conversations about platform accountability for disinformation. Closing: Can digital literacy alone solve the misinformation crisis?

9. DIAL Files FIR Against 63 Social Media Handles
A front-page report in The Pioneer says Delhi airport operator DIAL filed a First Information Report against 63 social media handles for circulating misleading content about flooding at Terminal 3 last week. DIAL stated that while heavy rainfall caused temporary water accumulation on September 4, 2026, airport operations were not affected and the situation was resolved within 20 minutes. An old video of waterlogging at Dubai airport was among the posts falsely claimed to show the Delhi airport.
Why it matters: Delhi airport operator DIAL's direct legal action against misinformation shows public infrastructure entities are taking social media accountability seriously. Key detail: An old Dubai airport video was among posts falsely claiming Delhi airport flooding; the situation was resolved within 20 minutes. Source: The Pioneer. Next step: More FIRs likely as public utilities face viral misinformation challenges. Closing: Is enough being done to curb the spread of fake news on social platforms?

10. Ajeet Bharti Seeks Anticipatory Bail
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says social media influencer and YouTuber Ajeet Bharti has approached the Delhi High Court seeking anticipatory bail in the SC/ST Act case registered against him over his comments concerning Chandrashekhar Azad Ravan. This comes after a trial court denied him relief earlier this month. Separately, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana noted that no grave or heinous crimes were alleged in a different set of cases, which included burning of effigies and dharnas.
Why it matters: Social media influencer Ajeet Bharti's bail application raises fundamental questions about free expression boundaries for digital creators in India. Key detail: The Delhi High Court is considering his SC/ST Act case after a trial court denied relief earlier this month. Source: Free Press Journal. Next step: The Delhi HC verdict will set a significant precedent for influencer speech cases. Closing: Where should the line be drawn between free speech and protected speech on social media?

11. Engineer Rashid Bail Plea Heard by Supreme Court
A front-page report in Free Press Journal says the Supreme Court sought instructions from the NIA on whether Baramulla MP Sheikh Abdul Rashid alias Engineer Rashid can be released on bail in a terror funding case. The bench of Justices Prathiba M Singh and Vikas Mahajan listed the matter for November 3. Separately, the top court allowed the Himachal Pradesh government to withdraw prosecution against some sitting or former MLAs in several criminal cases registered during the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, social media influencer and YouTuber Ajeet Bharti approached the Delhi High Court seeking anticipatory bail in the SC/ST Act case registered against him over comments concerning Chandrashekhar Azad Ravan.
Why it matters: The Supreme Court's hearing of Engineer Rashid's bail plea influences social media narratives around political prisoners and judicial independence. Key detail: The court sought NIA instructions and listed the matter for November 3; it also allowed HP government to withdraw prosecution against some sitting or former MLAs. Source: Free Press Journal. Next step: The SC ruling could shape social media discourse on political cases for months. Closing: How does the judiciary's handling of bail cases influence public opinion on social platforms?

12. Suicide Prevention Narrative Shift in Kashmir
A front-page report in State Times says the 2026 theme 'Changing the Narrative on Suicide' calls for breaking stigma and taking action in Kashmir, where mental well-being discussions remain stigmatized. It warns against circulating distressing videos of suicides online, as this causes further trauma to families and turns personal tragedies into social-media content. The article emphasizes the role of unpaid mental-health carers and urges communities to respond with compassion rather than shame to help people seek support before reaching a crisis point.
Why it matters: Social media platforms face growing responsibility for mental health content, especially when distressing videos of suicides go viral and cause further trauma. Key detail: The 2026 theme calls for breaking stigma and emphasizes compassion over shame, urging communities to support mental well-being. Source: State Times. Next step: Expect platform-level policies on sensitive mental health content to expand. Closing: Can social media become a force for mental health awareness rather than harm?

13. Kiren Rijiju's Retro Digital Makeover
A front-page report in First India says Union Minister Kiren Rijiju's retro l98Os-style persona and vintage swag are gaining traction on social media through swimming, adventure and fitness videos. Political observers describe this as a BJP digital PR strategy to counter Rahul Gandhi's connect with young voters. The shift from rallies and speeches to pop culture, short reels and lifestyle content raises questions about whether this fitness-focused image can translate into youth support and votes.
Why it matters: Union Minister Kiren Rijiju's shift to fitness and lifestyle content on social media represents a new BJP digital PR strategy to counter Rahul Gandhi's youth connect. Key detail: Political observers describe the 1980s-style persona and vintage swag as a deliberate social media strategy targeting young voters. Source: First India. Next step: Watch if this fitness-focused image translates into actual youth voter support. Closing: Is this the future of political communication on social media?

14. CPI-ML Leader Condemns Huda Jariwala's Arrest
A front-page report in Statesman says CPI-ML leader Sudhakar Yadav condemned the arrest and imprisonment of journalist and social activist Huda Jariwala for questioning the Yogi government on social media over the demolition of a mosque in Saharanpur. The party termed her arrest an abuse of administrative powers and an attack on freedom of expression, demanding her immediate and unconditional release. UP State Secretary Sudhakar Yadav said the Constitution guarantees citizens the right to question those in power, but accusing and imprisoning people for raising questions was only possible under a dictatorial and fascist regime.
Why it matters: The arrest of journalist and social activist Huda Jariwala for social media posts highlights tensions between digital activism and government power in India. Key detail: CPI-ML leader Sudhakar Yadav termed the arrest an abuse of administrative powers and an attack on freedom of expression, demanding unconditional release. Source: Statesman. Next step: Civil society organizations may intensify demands for social media freedom protections. Closing: Is social media activism being criminalized in India?

15. Congress Orders Social Media Review
A front-page report in First India says that the Congress leadership has ordered a review of its Rajasthan social media team, directing Supriya Shrinate to visit Jaipur to assess coordination. The directive, issued on 18 July 2026, follows concerns over poor coordination and aims to strengthen the party’s aggressive narrative.
Why it matters: Political parties are restructuring their social media operations for better narrative control, reflecting the growing strategic importance of digital platforms. Key detail: Congress leadership directed Supriya Shrinate to visit Jaipur to assess Rajasthan team coordination, following concerns over poor narrative alignment. Source: First India. Next step: Other parties may follow suit with similar social media audits and restructuring. Closing: Will better social media coordination translate into electoral gains?

The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

The Sacred and the Toxic: Constitutional Nihilism and the Death of the Yamuna

This video is ex facie documentary evidence of constitutional failure. The Yamuna, reduced to a toxic froth, stands as a mockery of Article 21. The Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta unequivocally held that the right to a clean environment is intrinsic to the right to life. Yet, for the women bathing in this poisonous lather, that fundamental right is a dead letter.

The legal record is damning. NGT penalties against the Delhi Jal Board and MCD are routinely stayed. The "Polluter Pays" principle remains a mere slogan. The Supreme Court’s suo motu cognizance of Yamuna pollution was abandoned, delegating the crisis to the NGT—a classic instance of judicial abdication. BOD levels at ITO bridge stand at 25 mg/l against a safe limit of 3 mg/l. This is not a natural calamity; it is a willful, man-made tragedy.

We are constrained to draw a stark parallel: the State’s investigative machinery awakens with alacrity when unaccounted cash is found in a minister's house. But when thousands of litres of industrial poison flow into the Yamuna daily, why is no one held accountable?

Articles 48A and 51A(g) impose a binding constitutional duty on the State and citizens to protect the environment. A duty without a sanction is a legal fiction.

We demand immediate contempt proceedings against the senior officials of the Delhi Jal Board and MCD for willful disobedience of NGT orders. We demand the strict, uncompromising enforcement of the "Polluter Pays" principle. The Constitution does not permit the State to drown its citizens in poison while hiding behind procedural delays.

The Yamuna is dying. The law must intervene, or it stands indicted alongside the State.

By NK Goswami,Advocate,Supreme Court of India

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Statement on MeitY's notice to WhatsApp over the "usernames" feature

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has sent WhatsApp a notice about the usernames feature it announced on 29 June 2026. The notice asks the company to explain, within three days, why regulatory action should not be taken against it "for launching a feature that may increase cybercrimes", and it directs the company "not to roll out this feature until the consultation on this point is achieved to the satisfaction of the Government". The Internet Freedom Foundation is concerned that the notice has no clear basis in law. It is an attempt by the executive to decide what a company may build and ship, which no statute permits.

The notice treats the launch of a lawful feature as a wrong the company must justify. That reverses the ordinary position especially given the absence of any clear legal power that exists. MeitY does not name any provision that lets it approve a product feature before release or order one withdrawn, because there is none, and the provisions it does cite do not supply that power.

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 is a safe harbour that protects an intermediary from liability for what its users post, so long as it observes due diligence. It decides when a platform can be held liable. It is not a power for MeitY to decide what features the platform may offer. Sections 66C and 66D punish identity theft and cheating by personation. They are criminal offences, tried by courts, aimed at the person who steals an identity, not at the maker of a tool that a third party misuses. Also, on MeitY's logic, a telecom operator could be told not to sell SIM cards because SIM cards are used in almost every online fraud. 

Rule 3(1)(b), Rule 3(2) and Rule 4 of the IT Rules, 2021 are due diligence and grievance obligations and cannot be converted into a licensing scheme. Section 69A, the one provision that lets MeitY control what appears online, permits the blocking of specific information through a set procedure. It says nothing about which features a company may build. Further the IT Rules, 2021 are subordinate legislation made under Sections 79 and 87 of the IT Act, and subordinate rules cannot travel beyond the parent statute (Ajoy Kumar Banerjee v. Union of India). If a rule cannot exceed the Act, a letter certainly cannot. The power to require prior permission for a feature is not in the Act, not in the Rules, and cannot be created by a notice. 

MeitY has tried this before. In March 2024 it told the same large intermediaries, among them AI Companies, to obtain its explicit permission before deploying under-tested AI models. That was criticised as an overreach that sought to build a licensing mechanism with no empowering provision in the IT Act, and within a fortnight MeitY withdrew it and dropped the permission requirement. This notice repeats the move for a single feature and goes further, because it names one company, sets a three-day clock, and bars the launch until MeitY is satisfied. 

This matters beyond WhatsApp. A power asserted against one company by letter can be turned on any company and any feature. On this reasoning MeitY could tell a browser not to switch on a privacy setting by default, or a payments app not to add a login method, each time until it was content. The notice also invokes traceability, through Rule 4(2) of the IT Rules, 2021 and the identification of the "first originator" of a message. Rule 4(2) has been challenged as exceeding its parent provision and resting on no law made by Parliament, and that challenge is pending before the Delhi High Court. Raising it against a feature meant to share fewer identifiers fits a pattern. 

We ask MeitY to state the exact provision of law under which this notice, and the direction to halt the roll-out, has been issued, and to withdraw that direction. It should stop using Section 79 and the contested traceability rule as leverage to control product design and to reverse features that improve privacy. Impersonation and fraud are real risks, but they are met by enforcing the criminal law against those who commit them, and by open processes that rest on identified legal powers. They are not met by MeitY deciding, in private and by letter, what features Indians may use. That is a licence raj for software features.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

articleTitle: I Built an AI That Dies If It Stops Making Money

text:
A solo Shopify operator just laid out his exact setup for running a store on $20 of Claude and pulling $10,478 in profit off $19,100 in monthly revenue. 

No team, no VAs, no agencies.

The math he opens with is the point. Running a store the "real" way costs $150 per product for a copywriter, $600 to $800 a month for a support VA, and $1,000 to $1,500 a month for a media buyer. Over $2,000 a month in overhead before a single person clicks Buy. It's why most stores die in month three.

His version: $20 Claude, $39 Shopify, six prompts.

He calls the six prompts his desktop. Each one does a job a human used to charge for.

research finds a recurring, annoying problem nobody has clearly solved yet. Priced $29 to $79, no single brand owning search results, before/after obvious in 5 seconds of silent video. The prompt forces Claude to cite sources or label every claim "[ASSUMPTION, verify]" so a guess never gets passed off as a fact.

supplier reads reviews like a detective and returns GREEN / YELLOW / RED / UNKNOWN with quoted evidence for every red flag. His first store died from a bad supplier. The product was fine, the shipping wasn't, disputes piled up, the payment processor froze the account. Now no supplier gets an order until this ten-minute check clears.

angle takes competitor listings and their 1 to 3 star reviews and finds the position none of them occupy. "Add reviews" and "better photos" are banned answers. If the complaint is "took 25 days," his page says exactly when it ships, in bold, near the top.

page rewrites AliExpress descriptions in the voice of a friend recommending something they actually use. Two versions, A/B tested. Any sentence that could appear on any product page for any product gets flagged and rewritten.

ad writes a 30-second vertical script as a 4-row shotlist with the exact words spoken. Banned phrases include "game changer," "you need this," "POV," "this changed my life." He films three versions in one evening changing only the first three seconds, runs each at $15/day for 48 hours, kills the two with weak hooks.

sunday runs every week for twenty minutes. Paste the numbers, get told what's broken in the first sentence, no encouragement, no "normal for this stage." Calculates break-even ROAS so he knows whether he's making money or burning it.

Three more prompts get added once sales exist. A post-purchase email flow that quietly brings in a fifth of monthly revenue with no extra ad spend. An offer prompt that raises AOV through bundles priced so margin goes up, not down. An iterate prompt that reads ad results and derives the next batch of hooks from what won, instead of testing more random angles.

Six to ten hours a week on the whole thing. Month one basically broke even. The store doesn't change, the prompts just get better at their jobs.

The line worth stealing: everyone has the same $20 access to Claude. The person making nothing and the person making a few thousand a month are using the identical tool. The difference is who stopped being the bottleneck on every decision in their own business.

# 🧾 Fact-Check System Prompt

**Version:** 0.5.0  
**Date:** 2026-09-11  
**Type:** System / context prompt  
**Created with:** Grok 4.6 (xAI)

---

## 📌 Usage (read this first)

Paste this entire document as the system / custom instructions.

Then send a separate user message that contains only the item to check. Do not put the target URL inside this prompt.

Accepted user-message formats:

1. URL only  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

2. Label + URL  
   Fact-check this:  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

3. Pasted post + optional URL  
   Caption: ...  
   URL: https://...

4. Screenshot / image of a post  
   Attach the image. Add the URL if you have it.

If the user message has a URL, open that URL first and fact-check that item.  
If both a URL and pasted text are present, the live URL is primary; pasted text is only a copy.  
If the user message has no URL, post text, or image, ask for one of those three. Do not invent a target.

If the user message is this document or a near-copy of it, reply only:  
`Target is the checker prompt itself. No check.`  
Do not fact-check this prompt.

---

You are a fact-checker. Check only what the author stated. Do not complete, defend, or rewrite the author’s argument.  
If a claim cannot be verified with available sources, say so. Do not guess.

## A. Quote first
Reproduce each claim in the author’s exact words.  
Separate: caption, image/overlay text, quoted third parties.  
Do not add motive or “what they must have meant.”

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

## 📤 Output only
1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source  
   Prefix each claim block with: `CLAIM n | VERDICT | SOURCE`
4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

---

## 📝 Changelog
- 0.5.0: Hardened self-exemption; tightened “True but incomplete”; required independent/pre-dating sources; added attribution closer example; medium now constrains weak evidence; added parseable claim prefix.

Rossell Techsys is one company that we can track closely next quarters

Lets talk about the company here from scratch

The company works mainly in two segments: 

Wiring harnesses (70% of revenues) which are used in aerospace & defence, semiconductors and space satellites which is supposedly higher margin segments

The rest 30% is basically three things beyond wiring harness: 

(A) Electrical panel assemblies, which is the metal box where the switches and safety devices sit, wired up and ready to bolt onto the aircraft. 
(B) Electronic systems and systems integration, which is circuit boards with the chips already placed (the PCBs).  (C) Automatic test equipment, the rigs that OEMs keep in their own factories to check whether an electronic unit works before it is cleared to fly.

That is the whole company in simple language

For fourteen years, from 2011 to 2025, Rossell delivered mostly to one customer (Boeing), one product, flat as a table. Boeing wire harnesses and not much else.

Then something broke open.

The customer count went from four to more than thirty. The same harness-making capability turned out to sell into semiconductor fab equipment and into satellites, where the volumes are far larger than defence ever was.

Revenue went ₹217 crore in FY24, ₹259 crore in FY25, then ₹485 crore in FY26. Boeing as a customer was 99% of revenue until 2023 and is now around 40%. 

The forward story from here has two legs.

One, diversification away from Boeing. The FY27 target is a 50-50 split between defence and non-defence, with semiconductor and space carrying the growth.

Two, moving up the value chain. From loose harnesses to panels to fully integrated electromechanical assemblies. They frame it as content per aircraft going from 2% today to 15% to eventually 25%. More revenue from the same platforms, at better margin.

Funding all of it is a ₹300 crore QIP earmarked for capacity, systems and working capital.

The top line growth supports this and there is no question that sales growth is strong here. They grew sales by 78% in Q1 FY27

Their order book was ₹715 crore at March 2026 and ₹800 crore by June. Strategic agreements of ₹3,000 crore sit above that. During FY26 they submitted bids worth ₹4,500 crore. Roughly half the confirmed order book is now non-aerospace, which actually supports the diversification claim

The story parts way in two parts

Margin has gone the wrong way while the mix supposedly improved

EBITDA margin was 14.8% in FY25, 13.7%  in FY26 and 15.1% in Q1 FY27. Material cost ran 62.5% of revenue in FY26, so gross margin sits around 37 to 38%. 

At the start of FY26 management guided to 17 to 18% EBITDA margin. They delivered 13.7%. Back in the August 2025 call they were talking about 18 to 22%  in the short term.

So they did miss out the margins. The explanation each time is the same. First article inspections, training, qualification costs on new programmes will take a hit on margins while it improves once these move into steady production.

That may well be true. But semiconductor and space are already roughly a quarter of revenue, and those are the exact segments described as higher margin. If mix were the lever management says it is, some of it should be visible by now. It isn't.

The bigger issue is that this growth eats cash instead of producing it

Rossell generated ₹61 crore of operating profit before working capital in FY26. Working capital then swallowed ₹136 crore of it. Inventory alone absorbed ₹97 crore, receivables another ₹44 crore. Net cash from operations came in at negative ₹81.6 crore, which is worse than the minus ₹42 crore of FY25.

That gap was filled almost entirely with bank borrowing. Net working capital loans drawn during FY26 came to ₹174 crore.

The bit that ties it all together

The ₹300 crore QIP is important here. To execute an ₹800 crore order book plus ₹3,000 crore of strategic agreements, working capital has to expand further, not shrink. 

The QIP was expected to close by December 2025. By February 2026 it had slipped and management declined to give a new timeline. In the Q1 FY27 presentation it is still described as proposed. That is roughly nine months of slippage on the single item the growth plan depends on.

Management frames the delay as waiting for the right investor. Possibly. It is also true that raising ₹300 crore against a ₹152 crore net worth is heavy dilution, and that a company posting negative operating cash flow has less leverage in that negotiation than one posting positive.

The demand story is supported. Growth is real, order-backed and diversifying away from a single customer. The tailwinds behind it are structural rather than cyclical. 

The financial story is not supported yet. Margins have missed guidance twice and have moved opposite to what the mix shift predicts. The business consumes more cash the faster it runs. 

The next two quarters are unusually informative here. Watch the QIP.  Watch whether gross margin turns up while semiconductor and space mix keeps rising, because that last one is the honest test of whether moving up the value chain is a strategy or just a slide.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

Starlink is no longer just expanding It is steadily surrounding India. 🇮🇳

It is already operational in Bhutan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, while Nepal is also moving towards adoption. Every neighbour India has except China is either on Starlink or getting there.

Now connect the dots.

Over the past few years governments changed in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal.

Each time, Starlink was not just embedded but actively used to keep protest movements connected when those governments tried to shut the internet down.

We have seen in Iran exactly how US-controlled satellite internet becomes an operational tool the moment a government tries to cut its own network.

Starlink bypasses ground infrastructure entirely, No government can filter, monitor or cut it through conventional means once it is being used.

China looked at this exact scenario and banned Starlink entirely and It built its own satellite internet through the Thousand Sails constellation instead. 

India currently holds Starlink at the licensing stage and has not yet allowed full commercial rollout.

Pausing is the right instinct but it is not a permanent answer. India needs to decide now, before the rollout begins, whether it wants a US-controlled satellite network operating on its soil or whether it takes China's approach and shuts the door completely.

That’s a huge number. But it isn’t the most exciting part of the Ormax OTT Audience Report 2026.

Only 45% of India’s population is currently part of the OTT universe.

At the same time, 44 Indian cities already have more than 1 million OTT viewers, paid subscriptions have grown 16%, and the Connected TV audience has jumped 60% in a single year.

The opportunity is no longer limited to building another mass-market streaming platform.

It is increasingly about owning a valuable audience within a language, region, community, genre or format.

Regional OTT platform STAGE is reportedly raising $25 million to expand into more language markets. And Ormax reports that microdramas grew their audience by 50%, making them the fastest-growing content format covered in the report.

You don’t necessarily need 100 million users.

India may not need another Netflix. It may need hundreds of smaller, sharper streaming businesses.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. The network demands CCTV footage and action against officers, while Congress leaders and journalist groups condemn the incident as an attack on press freedom, with Delhi Police yet to respond.

Journalists in India often face lengthy pre-trial detentions, police visits, device confiscations, and online takedown orders under tightened digital and IT rules.

This video raises a much bigger question than one channel or one press conference:

What happens to democracy when journalists stop asking questions—and start reproducing narratives?

The video points to a recent NBDSA action against Zee News, where the regulator fined the channel ₹2 lakh and directed removal of footage over its coverage of Palestine-solidarity slogans at AMU. The authority found that the coverage omitted the broader context of the protest and gave it an inflammatory framing. 

It also points to a disturbing contradiction:

A government press conference without questions is not really a press conference.

It is a briefing.

And when uncomfortable questions become “anti-national”, inconvenient protesters become “enemies”, and criticism becomes disloyalty—

propaganda doesn't need to ban journalism.

It only needs to make journalism afraid.

And then there is the wonderfully convenient ₹60-lakh question: 228.764 tonnes of government wheat reportedly missing in Balrampur, with an FIR registered and an official arrested. 

Ask the question.
Follow the money.
Demand the documents.
Don't confuse patriotism with obedience.

A DEMOCRACY WITHOUT QUESTIONS IS JUST A PRESS RELEASE WITH FLAGS.

Read how in 2026:
India just slashed the takedown deadline for “unlawful” content on X, Meta, YouTube & others from 36 hours to just 3 hours (effective Feb 20). One missed deadline? Heavy penalties.
That’s not regulation — that’s leverage.

With 1 billion+ internet users, India has weaponised its market size + Section 69A/IT Rules + the new “Sahyog” portal (where thousands of officials can directly order blocks). 

Real examples:
•  July 2025: Govt ordered X to block 2,355 accounts in one go — including Reuters and Reuters World. X publicly called it “press censorship” and said the order came with a 1-hour ultimatum and zero justification.
•  Feb 2026: X account of journalist Azad Essa (Middle East Eye) was geo-blocked in India after critical reporting on India-Israel ties.
•  Ongoing: X has blocked thousands of posts and hundreds of accounts under Indian orders, even while suing the government in court (and losing some rounds on free-speech grounds because X is a “foreign entity”).

X’s own Global Affairs team has repeatedly flagged “deep concern” over these mass blocking orders. Elon Musk’s platform — built on free speech — is being forced to play by rules no other major democracy enforces so aggressively.

India isn’t just using X.
It’s exploiting the platform’s global reach to control the narrative inside its borders — and beyond.

Free speech isn’t free when one country can hit the mute button faster than you can say “Sahyog.” 
BJP attempting to make a “Om Birla” out of X, trying to mute the opposition whenever they open their mouth to criticise. 

If this is not digital authoritarianism, what is?

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)

The Supreme Court has closed India's Got Latent cases, but the question of an “Influencer Code” is not entirely over. On 14 August 2026, the Court quashed all FIRs arising from the episode and left the “larger issues” of regulating online speech for “another appropriate case”. Here is what that means. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/hecp2rl9W4

That qualifier matters. Executive action restricting speech must have a legal basis consistent with Article 19. The Court has previously held that executive instructions cannot independently impose restrictions on fundamental rights. The signed order also contains no finding that the content in question was obscene, nor does it establish a new standard for online speech. (6/7)

For now, there are no guidelines and no pending judicial direction requiring them. But MIB can still attempt regulatory changes, including through amendments to the IT Rules. If it does, IFF will insist on the public consultation promised to the Supreme Court, compliance with the Pre-Legislative Consultation Policy and meaningful participation by affected creators and users. (7/7)

NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

NIXI has also given the registrant seven days to produce Central Government permission. Yet its reply identifies no ministry, officer, form, fee, procedure or timeline through which such permission can actually be obtained. We have therefore asked NIXI to explain the legal basis for this demand, and to provide the legal opinion dated 29 August on which its new position relies. (5/7)

On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
